t: A rejection is a list of reasons
l: The publisher approves an item, or sends it back with reasons the editor can act on one by one. Each reason is pinned to its field.
r: The publisher comments on the metadata row itself. Each comment becomes a reason that carries its field and a category.
Flagged rows stay marked on the page, so the editor resolves them in place instead of searching.
Before anything is sent, Reject shows how many reasons there are and who gets the item back.
Unflag removes a reason before it's sent, for when the publisher misread a field.

t: Treating region as a structural scope, not just a filter
l: Title, synopsis, age rating, dates, rights, audio and subtitles all change by region. The editor picks a region first, and the whole page answers for it.

t: Every level carries its own metadata
l: Series, season, episode, file: each level has its own fields and status, so nothing gets filed on the wrong one.

t: The editor never hunts for what is missing
l: What the region still needs sits at the top, above everything the upload already filled.
r: The readiness panel lists what must be complete before the season can be scheduled in this region.
“4 of 8” tells the editor how much is left and where to start. “Incomplete” only says something is wrong.
Every empty field is grouped in “Needs your input”, above what the upload already filled.
Values read from the file, like runtime and codec, can't be edited. Values from the delivery unlock one field at a time.
Submit hands the episode to the publisher. Save keeps it under In progress, ready to pick up later.

l: The AI points at likely rejections before the publisher sees them. It never fills a field: a wrong auto-fill is an error nobody notices.
r: The AI learns from past rejection reasons. Every reason carries a field and a category, so they can be counted per team and per region.
A broken rule is a failed check, never a guess. The AI only raises judgement calls and says how sure it is.
A flag opens its field, or gets dismissed with a reason that stays on record.

t: Designed for the delivery that arrives broken
l: Deliveries often arrive incomplete or mislabelled. After upload, the system assigns the files it can match and hands the rest to the editor.
r: Processing reads each file’s technical metadata and matches it to its content, so most files are assigned automatically. Only the ones it cannot place wait for the editor.
24 uploaded, 9 assigned automatically, 15 for the editor: the whole result in one line.
The drop zone stays, so files can be added mid-upload.
Files keep their own states (Uploading, Processing, Ready, Needs assignment, Failed), separate from the workflow status of their content.

t: Every file sits under the content it belongs to
l: A missing file shows up as a gap on its title, before the delivery gets rejected.
r: Each film or episode shows its file count, like 2 of 7.
Two views: Content groups files under their film or episode, Files lists them all for bulk work. Language and Type are filters, not groupings.

t: Artwork is chosen by taste, not by country
l: Most viewing starts from a recommendation, so the thumbnail does much of the selling. Taste predicts a click better than age or location, so each season carries one thumbnail per taste cluster.
r: Action, drama, romance and mystery fans each see the scene most likely to make them click.
Variants are tested against each other in each region, with the time left on the test, so the editor knows when the artwork is final.
Each variant shows its click-through rate, and the leader is marked.

t: The queue is sorted by what airs first
l: The episode that airs first sits on top. Each row offers only what its status allows: Review while it waits, Publish once approved.

t: Once review starts, content is locked
l: After approval, a change needs an edit request. It's for news from outside, like a new regional age rating. Fixing approved work isn't what it's for.
